title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome secondary to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in a child: a case report from the Tibetan plateau
case_prompt:
A 14-year-old Tibetan girl presented with multiple tonic–clonic seizures for 14 hours and progressive headache for 2 weeks accompanied by dizziness and vomiting. She had a 1-month history of haematuria, fever, and pharyngalgia. There was no prior history of hypertension, diabetes, head injury, or drug allergies. On examination, her blood pressure was 150/90 mmHg; she was somnolent, had facial swelling, and muscle strength was grade 4/5 in all four limbs.  
Urinalysis showed 3+ haematuria, 3+ proteinuria, and 1+ leukocyturia. Blood tests revealed urea nitrogen 7.33 mmol/L, serum creatinine 168 μmol/L, WBC 10 770 cells/mm3, C-reactive protein 40.44 mg/L, hypersensitive CRP 10 mg/L, haemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, anti-streptolysin O antibody 890.4 IU/mL, and antinuclear antibody titre 1:1280.  
Brain T2-FLAIR MRI demonstrated bilateral hyperintense signals in the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes. DWI showed slight hyperintensity in the bilateral frontal cortex and hypointensity in the right occipital lobe. Brain CT revealed corresponding bilateral hypodense lesions. A renal ultrasound showed enhanced echoes in both kidneys. Chest CT showed right-sided pneumonia.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was most consistent with the acute neurologic presentation and characteristic imaging of vasogenic oedema — “PRES was diagnosed on the basis of both an acute onset of multiple neurologic features and distinctive neuroimaging findings.”  
2. Ischaemic stroke was considered due to focal neurologic deficits but was ruled out — “Differential diagnoses of ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, infectious encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, high-altitude cerebral oedema and central nervous system vasculitis were ruled out.”  
3. Cerebral venous thrombosis was considered but was ruled out — “Differential diagnoses of ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, infectious encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, high-altitude cerebral oedema and central nervous system vasculitis were ruled out.”  
4. Infectious encephalitis was considered but was ruled out — “Differential diagnoses of ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, infectious encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, high-altitude cerebral oedema and central nervous system vasculitis were ruled out.”  
5. Autoimmune encephalitis was considered but was ruled out — “Differential diagnoses of ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, infectious encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, high-altitude cerebral oedema and central nervous system vasculitis were ruled out.”  
6. High-altitude cerebral oedema was considered given the setting but was ruled out — “Differential diagnoses of ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, infectious encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, high-altitude cerebral oedema and central nervous system vasculitis were ruled out.”  
7. Central nervous system vasculitis was considered but was ruled out — “Differential diagnoses of ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, infectious encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, high-altitude cerebral oedema and central nervous system vasculitis were ruled out.”
